correctness.rationale: The frequency group and unnormalized Walsh transform are explicitly specified. The key dyadic-block induction pairs complementary half-position vertex sets, whose cross signs sum to 0 or plus/minus 2; each internal factor has the inductive divisor. Binary-position-block decomposition gives \(2^{n-s_2(n)}\) for all signs. Character orthogonality at the identity orientation forces the gcd to divide \(2^{\binom n2}\), and \(W_n(0)=n!\) fixes its exact exponent by Legendre valuation. Order reversal proves odd-weight Walsh zeros. Checked exact signed enumeration/fast Walsh transforms for \(n\\le6\) and deterministic sign samples \(n=7,8\). No numerical test is used as proof of the infinite claim.

evidence: The published research result “Integral tight Fourier sampling and tree-complement designs for regular tournaments” analyzes a regular-tournament sampling subspace and its Gram determinants; its object differs from the all-transitive-orientation indicator and gcd.

The result “Factorial acyclic signatures for complete graphs minus a matching” concerns a fixed family of near-complete graph acyclic-orientation signature imbalances, not arbitrary edge-character evaluation of every transitive tournament.

equivalent_formulations.reasoning: The Walsh coefficient equals the graphical-inversion polynomial at minus one for the arbitrary graph encoded by the negative frequency coordinates. The papers develop the common language, but their stated all-graph conclusions concern equidistribution, not the exact common two-adic divisor across all graphs. The usual q-factorial is only the complete-graph special evaluation, which vanishes at minus one and therefore does not give the gcd.

value.rationale: The exact gcd of all Fourier coefficients of a canonical infinite family of transitive tournament indicators is a natural arithmetic spectral invariant, not an arbitrary slice. It gives the strongest universal spectral quantization at every n, grows as \(2^{n-s_2(n)}\), and supplies an all-n bound for inverses on the nonzero Fourier subspace. The complementary-block argument is a structural lemma that applies to every arbitrary comparison sign graph. The claim does not pretend to determine the exact nonzero gap or full rank.
